hints: Think about what is different between an alternating supply that keeps changing direction and a direct supply that flows one way only - what change must rectification make?
walkthrough:
**Picture a.c. versus d.c.**
Think of a.c. as pushing then pulling, with voltage swinging positive then negative. Think of d.c. as pushing in one direction only. Rectification is the process that turns that two-way variation into a one-way output.
Final answer: the conversion of alternating current or voltage to direct current or voltage

hints: Focus on what happens to the half of the a.c. cycle that is in the unwanted direction - is it simply lost or is it kept in some way?
Compare blocking one polarity completely with flipping one polarity over so both halves end up on the same side.
walkthrough:
**Half-wave means half is missing**
With a single diode, current can pass one way but not the other. So for one half-cycle you get an output, for the next half-cycle you get zero. One direction is removed.

**Full-wave means nothing is wasted**
With a bridge of diodes, the negative half-cycle is not blocked, it is turned upside down. Both positive and negative input halves give a positive output, so you get twice as many pulses.

Final answer: In half-wave rectification the voltage of one polarity is removed (blocked), so output exists for only half of each cycle. In full-wave rectification the voltage of one polarity is reversed, so both halves of each cycle appear as output in the same direction.

hints: For half-wave you need current to reach the resistor on only one half-cycle - where must a one-way device go to control the whole output?
Remember one input lead can go straight through to the output side, but the other lead needs the diode in series, drawn as a triangle pointing toward a bar.
walkthrough:
**Place the diode in series**
You have two gaps between $V_{IN}$ on the left and the C-R parallel combination on the right. Leave the bottom gap as a plain wire. Put a single diode in the top gap so all current to the resistor must go through it.

**Use the correct symbol**
Draw the diode as a triangle with its point touching a short bar: $\triangleright |$. Either orientation gives half-wave action, it just selects which half-cycle is passed. This allows conduction in one direction only and blocks the opposite half-cycle.

Final answer: Connect one $V_{IN}$ lead directly to the lower common line of C and R. Connect the other $V_{IN}$ lead to the upper common line of C and R through a single diode in series, using the correct diode symbol.

hints: Look at where C is connected - directly across R - and think about what a capacitor does when the rectified voltage tries to fall to zero.
walkthrough:
**Capacitor as a reservoir**
The capacitor charges up to the peak rectified voltage. When the diode stops conducting and the supply would drop to zero, the capacitor discharges through R, keeping $V_{OUT}$ high. That smooths the pulses into a steadier d.c. voltage.
Final answer: Smoothing - to store charge when $V_{OUT}$ is high and release it when $V_{OUT}$ would otherwise fall, reducing variation (ripple) in $V_{OUT}$.

hints: Start from Fig. 6.3 and identify the maximum value of $V_{OUT}$ - this is the voltage across C when it stores maximum energy.
Link stored energy to capacitance and that peak voltage, then rearrange to find $C$ and convert to $\mu\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
**Read the peak voltage**
From Fig. 6.3 the maximum $V_{OUT}$ is $12\text{ V}$. This is the voltage across the parallel capacitor at maximum charge, so use $V = 12\text{ V}$ and $E = 0.041\text{ J}$.

**Rearrange and calculate**
Energy in a capacitor is $$E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$ so $$C = \frac{2E}{V^2}$$ Substituting: $$C = \frac{2 \times 0.041}{12^2} = \frac{0.082}{144} \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ Since $1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}$, this is about $570\,\mu\text{F}$, as required.

hints: Look at Fig. 6.3 for a discharge section where $V_{OUT}$ falls smoothly - what are the start voltage, end voltage and time taken for that fall?
Recall how voltage decays with time when a capacitor discharges through a resistor, and think about which time interval corresponds to $t$ in that relation.
Take natural logs to isolate $R$, using your value of $C \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$ from (c)(i).
walkthrough:
**Spot the discharge**
From $t = 0.01\text{ s}$ to $t = 0.02\text{ s}$ in Fig. 6.3, $V_{IN}$ is negative so the diode blocks and C discharges through R. Voltage falls from $V_0 = 12\text{ V}$ to $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ in time $t = 0.010\text{ s}$.

**Apply exponential discharge**
For discharge: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{RC}\right)$$ So: $$8.0 = 12.0 \exp\left(-\frac{0.010}{RC}\right)$$
Final answer: $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ with $V_0 = 12.0\text{ V}$ falling to $8.0\text{ V}$ in $t = 0.010\text{ s}$ gives $R \approx 43\,\Omega$.
